Kielce Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kielce, Poland

Not demolished. Kielce's Jewish community, established in the second half of the 19th century, grew to 15,530 people by 1921, most killed by the Germans in 1942. On July 4, 1946 — after the war's end — a pogrom took place in Kielce that caused around 70,000 Holocaust survivors to flee Poland in the following months, one of the most consequential postwar events in European Jewish history. This cemetery, established in 1868, is the burial place of four tzaddikim: Chaim Szmuel Horowitz of Chęciny, great-grandson of the Seer of Lublin (died 1913); Motele Twerski of the Chernobyl dynasty, documented elsewhere in this collection (died 1917); Ozer Abraham Rabinowicz (died 1925); and Elimelech Jakow Rabinowicz (died 1938). Victims of the 1946 pogrom were buried here on July 8 of that year. In 2007, the Hasidic community recovered and renovated Motele Twerski's ohel, and in 2010, at the initiative of the Jan Karski Association, a new monument was erected on the pogrom victims' grave.
